analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal student aid law, easing rules on for-profit colleges while ending several loan forgiveness and grant programs.
analysis.headline: The House passed it out of committee on a party-line vote but never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The PROSPER Act was the House Republicans' rewrite of the Higher Education Act. It would have replaced the existing student loan programs with a single new loan and one income-based repayment plan, simplified the financial aid application, and created a college information dashboard. At the same time it repealed rules that hold career-education programs accountable for whether graduates can find work, barred the Education Department from writing those rules again, ended Public Service Loan Forgiveness and other loan forgiveness programs for new borrowers, and repealed the Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant. It cleared the House committee on a party-line vote but was never brought to the House floor, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: For-profit and online colleges gain most: the bill repeals the gainful employment rule (which cut aid to career programs whose graduates could not repay loans), repeals the 2016 borrower-defense regulations that let cheated students cancel loans, prohibits the Education Department from ever writing gainful-employment rules or rating colleges, and removes long-standing restrictions on federal aid flowing to for-profit and correspondence institutions. It also eliminates loan forgiveness for public-service workers and several grant programs, sparing the federal budget those costs. Students who borrow get a single loan program, one income-based repayment plan, and a simplified aid application.

how_it_helps.text: It consolidated the two existing federal student loan programs into a single loan program and replaced multiple repayment plans with one income-based plan, making repayment simpler to understand.
It simplified the FAFSA financial-aid application and set, for the first time, clear borrowing limits for graduate students.

It expanded the College Dashboard consumer website to show, by program, graduation rates, borrowing, debt levels, and graduates' earnings, and required every college to post a standardized net price calculator.
It authorized an apprenticeship grant program and reauthorized Pell Grants, work-study, TRIO, and aid for minority-serving institutions.

analysis.who_pays: Future students lose Public Service Loan Forgiveness, other loan forgiveness programs, and the Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant, and lose borrower-defense and gainful-employment protections against low-quality programs; low-income students lose access to some grant aid.

drawbacks.text: The bill repealed the 'gainful employment' rules and banned the Education Department from ever writing them again, taking away the main tool used to judge whether career education programs leave students able to repay their loans.

It repealed the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program and the Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant for new borrowers, cutting off debt relief for teachers, public defenders, and other public-service workers and grant aid for low-income students.

It repealed the 2016 borrower-defense regulations that let cheated students have their federal loans canceled, and replaced the existing Direct Loan program with a single new loan program with new limits and a single income-based repayment plan, shifting repayment terms for millions of borrowers.
It sharply limited the Education Department's authority to write rules and barred any institution rating system, reducing oversight of colleges that receive federal money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's simplification and consolidation goals were real improvements, but they came bundled with the wholesale repeal of the gainful employment and borrower-defense rules and the end of Public Service Loan Forgiveness for new borrowers — a package whose largest beneficiaries were the institutions the prior rules were written to police. An honest reauthorization could have simplified aid without dismantling accountability; this bill did not.

outcome.mechanism: The House education committee approved it on a party-line vote in December 2017 and formally reported it in February 2018, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced December 1, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On December 13, 2017, the committee ordered it reported as amended by a vote of 23 to 17, along party lines.
The committee formally reported the bill with House Report 115-550 on February 8, 2018, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting a floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Students and borrowers who would have lost loan forgiveness and borrower-defense protections kept them, since the bill never became law; the for-profit college industry failed to get the accountability rollback it sought through this bill, though it pursued it through regulation in the meantime.

for.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
for.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through her committee, which ordered it reported 23 to 17.

for.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted to report the bill out of committee.

against.name: 17 House committee Democrats
against.role: House Education and the Workforce Committee minority
against.what_they_did: Voted against the bill when the committee ordered it reported, 23 to 17.

against.name: Student, consumer, and civil rights groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill's repeal of gainful employment, borrower-defense, and loan forgiveness provisions.

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.role: Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Advanced no companion bill, leaving no reauthorization vehicle to consider.

sides.party_line_note: Every recorded vote on the bill split by party: the 23-17 committee vote to report it followed party lines, and all 21 cosponsors were Republicans.

industries.note: The bill repealed the gainful employment and borrower-defense rules, ended state-authorization and credit-hour regulations, and removed restrictions on federal aid to for-profit institutions and correspondence programs — removing the accountability framework those schools had fought for years.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and the Direct Loan program infrastructure
industries.note: The bill terminated the Federal Direct Loan program and replaced it with a new single loan program, requiring a wind-down and restructuring of the existing loan delivery system.

Institutions gained lighter regulation, less federal rulemaking, and new program-level earnings data they had not previously had to report, while losing the ability to shape accreditation and oversight through regulation; minority-serving institutions kept dedicated aid programs.

industries.industry: Public-service employers relying on loan forgiveness to recruit
industries.note: Repealing Public Service Loan Forgiveness for new borrowers removed a tool schools, governments, and nonprofits use to attract workers into lower-paying public-service jobs.
